objection: Could the Bible have been changed to make Jesus divine?
answer: That's a really honest question, and I'm glad you're asking it rather than just assuming the worst—it deserves a careful answer, not a defensive one. Here's the key fact: we don't have to guess whether later editors smoothed over the "rough edges" of Jesus praying to the Father or crying out in anguish, because we have manuscript evidence reaching back astonishingly close to the events themselves. The Rylands fragment (P52) of John's Gospel dates to about AD 125, and P66 and P75 (c. 200) already preserve John's Gospel—including "the Word was God" (John 1:1) and Thomas' "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28)—more than a century before Nicaea ever met [11-xii-the-manuscript-and-textual-witness]. If someone wanted to erase the "human" Jesus who prays and suffers, they'd have had to do it before these papyri were copied, and yet the very same manuscripts that preserve his cries of forsakenness and his prayers to the Father are the ones preserving the highest claims about his deity, sitting side by side. That's the real pattern in the earliest texts: not a smoothing-over, but a deliberate holding-together of full humanity and full deity, because that's what the first Christians actually believed, not what later councils invented. Larry Hurtado's and Richard Bauckham's research shows this devotion to Jesus as sharing the divine identity erupted among Jewish believers within the first few years of the church, not centuries later [10-xi-how-early-is-this-belief]. So the "rough edges" you're noticing aren't accidents that slipped past an editor—they're original, load-bearing parts of the earliest portrait, the ones the doctrine of the incarnation was built to explain, not hide.

transcript.content: I appreciate you setting that up—that's exactly the kind of thing I worry about when I'm reading. Here's what nags at me: if the earliest Christians really did see Jesus as just a teacher, and then later councils and editors wanted to make him *divine*, couldn't they have... well, smoothed over the rough edges? Changed the places where he says "why have you forsaken me?" or where he prays *to* God, or where he asks for someone to be greater than him? It feels like the kind of thing that *could* have happened in copying—I mean, people make mistakes, and people also have reasons to change things. How do we actually *know* the texts we have now weren't shaped to fit what later Christians wanted to believe?

That's a fair worry, and it's actually one that's testable rather than merely speculative—which is good news. Here's the key point: the "rough edges" you mention (the cry of dereliction, Jesus praying to the Father, the Father being "greater") were never smoothed over. If later editors were shaping the text to fit a growing belief in Jesus's deity, those are exactly the verses we'd expect them to *cut*, not preserve. Instead they survive intact in our earliest manuscripts—P52 of John dates to around AD 125, and P66/P75 (c. 200) already contain "the Word was God" (John 1:1) and Thomas's confession "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), a century before Nicaea. The New Testament is the best-attested text from the ancient world, with over 5,800 Greek manuscripts, so we're not reconstructing it from late, tampered copies—we have a documentary trail reaching back almost to living memory of the events themselves.

And notice what this trail shows: the "hard" texts and the "high" texts sit side by side in the very earliest layers. That's because they were never in tension for the first Christians. The Son who says "why hast thou forsaken me" (Matthew 27:46) and the Son who is worshipped as God are the same person in two natures—true God, true man. Scholars like Hurtado and Bauckham have shown that worship of Jesus as sharing the divine identity erupted among Jewish believers within the earliest years, not as a late Gentile corruption. So the evidence doesn't support a story of gradual editing toward divinity; it supports a Jesus who was confessed as Lord and God from the very start, precisely alongside the texts you're worried might have been erased.
